analysis.one_liner: Moves the consumer financial watchdog's funding from automatic Federal Reserve money to annual congressional approval.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote, dying there when the 116th Congress ended with 42 Republican cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the federal agency that polices payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit card companies, is funded by transfers from Federal Reserve earnings rather than by annual congressional appropriations. This bill would strip that funding stream and instead require Congress to approve the CFPB's budget every year, capping authorizations for fiscal 2019 and 2020. The practical effect is that the financial industry's allies in Congress could shrink or zero out the watchdog's budget. The bill never moved after its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday lenders, debt collectors, and other financial companies regulated by the CFPB. Putting the bureau's budget under annual congressional control would open its funding to negotiation with lawmakers, many of whom receive industry support, making enforcement budgets easier to cut. Sponsors framed it as accountability for an agency that spends money without annual congressional review.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the CFPB's funding through Federal Reserve earnings transfers, the channel that lets the bureau operate outside the annual appropriations process.
It requires the bureau to be funded through regular appropriations, with authorizations capped for fiscal years 2019 and 2020, giving Congress annual control over how much the CFPB may spend.

Under current law, Congress cannot use the budget process to limit the CFPB's spending or enforcement capacity, which the bill's sponsors characterized as unaccountable spending by an unelected agency.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers who rely on the CFPB for refunds, enforcement actions, and complaints against payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit card companies. An annual appropriations fight over the bureau's budget would give regulated industries a recurring opportunity to weaken the cop on their beat.

drawbacks.text: Moving the CFPB into annual appropriations would hand Congress direct power to cut the bureau's budget, and critics say that power would be used by allies of the financial industry to blunt enforcement against predatory lending and debt collection practices.

The bill caps its authorization at only two fiscal years (2019 and 2020), so if the funding structure were never revisited the bureau's legal authorization would lapse, an added point of pressure beyond the annual fight itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — subjecting an agency's budget to elected officials — is a fair accountability argument in the abstract, and most agencies do face appropriations. But the CFPB's independent funding was designed deliberately so the financial industry could not choke off the agency policing it through the budget process. The bill's main practical effect would be to give that industry a recurring lever over its own regulator, and the cost would fall on consumers in the form of weaker enforcement and fewer refunds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr (R-KY) introduced the bill on February 5, 2019, with 28 original cosponsors, all Republicans.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, the only committee action it ever received.
Forty-two Republicans in total cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The House Financial Services Committee, controlled by Democrats that Congress, never took the bill up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead: the CFPB's independent funding stream, which shields the consumer watchdog from budget-pressure campaigns by the industries it regulates, survived this attempt to subject it to congressional appropriations. The financial companies that would have gained that lever came up empty.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, since CFPB funding independence survived

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 original Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 42 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat joined.

for.name: Banking and consumer finance industry groups
for.role: Regulated industries seeking congressional control over the CFPB budget
for.what_they_did: Long pushed for the CFPB to be funded through annual appropriations rather than automatic Federal Reserve transfers, giving Congress a budget lever over the bureau.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill, leaving it in committee until it expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 43 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans (43 of 197); no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic committee chair buried it without action.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer credit companies (payday lenders, debt collectors)
industries.note: The bill would give Congress annual control over the budget of the agency that enforces consumer financial rules against them, creating a recurring opportunity to shrink its enforcement. Their gain comes directly at the cost of consumer protections.
The bill would end the Fed's obligation to transfer earnings to fund the CFPB. The Fed loses a mandated expense but this has little practical effect on its operations or on consumers.
